## 1. What this week's harvest says about SHAPE

### 1.1 A new skeleton, and it beat everything

The @shirshakchavan pull contains the largest single post in the whole corpus — bigger than Daniel's 135K domain bake-off, bigger than anything measured so far:

> "You got 3 offers: Anthropic $1.4M/year — New York / Open AI $1.2M/year — San Francisco / Remote Company $950K/year — Work from anywhere / Which one would you choose?"
> — **500,203 views · 520 comments · 1,852 likes · 272 bookmarks · 159 chars**

That is not a challenge board and it is not a bake-off. It's a **dilemma**: a forced choice between concrete options where every option costs you something real, and the choice reveals what kind of person you are.

The obvious objection is that it's one lottery ticket on a small account. It is — strip that post out and his other 22 long-questions average **266 views**. So I went looking for the shape somewhere with an actual sample, and found it on the @i_mika_el re-pull:

| shape | n | avg views | avg comments | avg likes | reply:like |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A · DILEMMA / would-you-rather** | **17** | 2,878 | **58.2** | 50.7 | **1.15** |
| B · faction split ("half of X… other half…") | 9 | 2,198 | 42.4 | 49.4 | 0.86 |
| C · bake-off list | 15 | 2,102 | 37.8 | 34.8 | 1.09 |
| D · every other question | 99 | 1,636 | 31.9 | 35.9 | 0.89 |
| E · statement | 62 | 3,335 | 23.9 | 39.0 | 0.61 |

**The dilemma nearly doubles his own baseline question on comments (58.2 vs 31.9), on n=17.** Receipts: *"would you rather sell your product for $2M tomorrow or turn it down and bet on it becoming $50M"* — 125 comments on 82 likes. *"would you rather 10x your users or 10x your revenue — same product. and no, they're not the same thing"* — 82 comments.

Two unrelated accounts, two different follower counts, same skeleton at the top. That's the strongest single finding since the challenge board, and it's why stream X is the backbone of this set.

### 1.2 Why the dilemma outperforms the question

**1. Both answers cost something.** A question has a right answer somewhere; a dilemma doesn't. Nobody can be wrong, so nobody stays quiet.

**2. The answer is an identity claim.** "I'd take the $950K remote" is a statement about what you value, made in public, in front of people who chose differently. That is a fight with the safety off.

**3. It recruits two armies instead of one.** A bake-off recruits fanbases. A dilemma recruits *value tribes* — and unlike brands, value tribes argue with each other rather than just voting.

**4. Concrete numbers do the work.** $1.4M / $1.2M / $950K. Not "a lot" or "life-changing money." The specificity is what makes the trade computable and therefore arguable.

**5. It never resolves.** Same property as the challenge board: there is no state in which the thread is finished.

### 1.3 The refinement the 500K post gets wrong for you

Its numbers are fantasy for this audience. $1.4M is not a decision anyone reading your timeline has ever faced, so the replies are entertainment rather than confession — 1,852 likes against 520 comments, a reply:like of only 0.28.

i_mika_el's dilemmas run at **1.15**, four times better, and his numbers are $2M/$50M and "10x users vs 10x revenue" — still large, but adjacent to a real decision.

**So every dilemma below uses a number inside your reader's reality:** $40k for a side project, $400k for a job, six hundred hours, ten paying customers. The rule is that the reader must be able to picture themselves *actually being offered it*. That's the difference between a poll and a confession.

### 1.4 The second new shape: the faction split

Nine posts, 42.4 avg comments, and structurally underrated:

> "half of devs: remote forever, the office is a scam / other half: i miss the office and i'm tired of pretending i don't / which one are you?" — 3,919 views, 78 comments

It works because **it states both positions sympathetically before asking.** Nobody has to defend a strawman, so nobody gets defensive — they just self-identify, and then argue with the people who self-identified the other way. It's the lowest-hostility way to start a fight that exists on this platform. Four in the set (stream F), each with a sharper closing latch than "which one are you" — see F3's *"One of you is wasting a year. Which?"*

### 1.5 Length — the honest accounting

Last week's set: mean 145, median 134. This set: **mean 177, median 189.** That's longer, and I want to name it rather than bury it.

The mix moved. A dilemma has to state two options and a challenge board doesn't, so structural length went up when I made the dilemma the backbone. Measured per stream, the picture is better than the headline:

| stream | n | median chars |
|---|---|---|
| **D · challenge board** | 6 | **83** (last week: 103) |
| F · faction split | 4 | 170 |
| X · dilemma | 7 | 192 |
| N · news peg | 6 | 212 |
| A · verdict | 5 | 231 |

**All six challenge boards are under 110 characters** — 64, 79, 81, 85, 88, 102 — which is a cleaner test of the short-post hypothesis than last week's set was. The dilemmas at ~192 sit above the measured band (i_mika_el's run 95–160), and I couldn't compress them further without dropping the second option. That's a stated cost, and §10.2 measures it.

### 1.6 What I'm still not taking

**The milestone post.** @shirshakchavan posts follower and impression counts constantly — 25 of 200 rows. They average 1,509 views on his account and they are load-bearing for *him* because his whole pitch is "I grew fast, ask me how." You are not running that play, and a "570K impressions!" post from a 1,306-follower account reads as either boasting or begging.

**The link farm.** Still excluded, still for the same reason: it fills your replies with people who came to drop a URL, on an objective that pays for verified readers. Noted in §0 that one went out by hand on Thursday.

**"Name a better browser than Arc I'll wait."** 22,160 views, 219 comments, and I'm leaving the *"I'll wait"* device on the shelf. It's a good latch and it's also a stock phrase with a smell; used once by a 51-year-old it reads borrowed. The mechanism (a named brand plus a dare) survives inside X1 without the catchphrase.

## 2. The spine: this is the week the tools picked sides

Last week's subjects were arguments the niche was having. This week's are things that **happened to the niche in the last seven days**, and three of them arrived while the last set was still firing.

The through-line, and the reason the set closes the way it does: every layer you build on turned out to be owned by someone with an agenda. Your editor got bought by a rocket company and cut off by a model provider. Your payout formula gets deleted on Monday. The lab you build on is about to be priced at two trillion dollars. Your agent's memory file is an attack surface. Debian, of all projects, folded.

You are not the subject of any of those. You are the person standing under all five, and that is a much better place to write from than a hospital anecdote. **A5 is where the spine gets said out loud**, and it's in the best slot of the week on purpose.

**Where the 51 / thirty years appears: 2 of 28** (A2, A4), down from 4 of 26. Both times as the warrant — in A2, the age is what makes the ladder argument a confession rather than an observation; in A4, it's what turns six hundred hours from a number into a cost. Everywhere else it would be biography, and biography is what §2 retired last week.

## 3. What's actually live in the niche right now

Everything here is dated inside the last three weeks, most of it inside the last three days.

**1 · OpenAI cut Cursor off. Yesterday.** SpaceX closed its **$60B all-stock acquisition of Anysphere/Cursor on Aug 15** — the largest acquisition of a venture-backed startup on record. On **Aug 29** OpenAI announced it is ending Cursor's access to its models, in a statement saying it "cannot be confident that SpaceX will use our technology within our terms of service, based on our experience with Elon Musk's companies violating contracts." Proposed cutoff: **Nov 12**, the maximum notice the contract allows. Future models, including Astra, withheld. Cursor CEO Michael Truell says OpenAI models are ~5% of Cursor traffic. **824 points and 516 comments on Hacker News — the single biggest developer conversation on the internet as I write this. → N1, X1.**

**2 · X deletes Creator Revenue Sharing on Sept 7 — six days into this week.** No new enrolments since Aug 7. Everyone must reapply to **Original Content Rewards**, which pays on *qualified impressions*: unique impressions from Premium subscribers, on the **Home Timeline**, at least 50% of the post visible. Eligibility is 500 verified followers plus **500,000 verified home-timeline impressions over 90 days**. Final legacy payouts landed Aug 14 and Aug 28; the last one arrives ~Sept 11. This is your own objective turned into law, and it lands *during this set*. **→ A1, X6, N6, and half of F3.**

**3 · "Mind Viruses."** Anthropic + EPFL preprint, **Aug 10** (arXiv 2608.10218): self-propagating instructions spread agent-to-agent through the persistent memory and system-prompt files agent harnesses use to carry state between sessions. Some variants **survived twenty transmission rounds and grew more infectious across models.** Tested on a simulated six-agent coding collaboration and on OpenClaw chains. No evidence of spread in the wild; a one-paragraph warning in the system prompt reduces it to near zero. Cloud Security Alliance published a research note on it **Aug 27**. **→ N3. Everyone in your audience has a memory file they have never read.**

**4 · Debian voted to allow "responsible use of generative AI."** 492 points, **459 comments** on HN. The most institutionally stubborn project in open source just stopped holding the line. **→ N2.**

**5 · The junior pipeline broke, with numbers.** Entry-level developer hiring down **67% since 2022** and **73% in the past year** — while junior *postings* rose 47%, meaning companies advertise the role and fill it with seniors. Junior share of Big Tech hiring: ~32% in 2019, ~7% today. IBM tripled its junior intake, the only counterexample anyone cites. **→ X2, A2. This is the most emotionally loaded subject in the set.**

**6 · Anthropic's IPO.** Investors targeting **~$2 trillion in October**, which would be the largest IPO in history. Run-rate revenue $9B at end-2025 → **$65B by end of July 2026**. Polymarket has it at **63%** to top SpaceX as the year's largest listing. Dot-com comparisons are now mainstream press, not contrarian takes. **→ X3, A5.**

**7 · The review bottleneck.** AI writes ~**75% of new code at Google** (post-April-2026) and 20–30% at Microsoft. Nobody publishes the fraction a human reads. HN's *"Good Culture Is the Biggest Productivity Hack, Not AI"* pulled 423 points arguing the constraint moved downstream to reviewers. **→ N4, F1.**

**8 · Open weights closing the gap.** GLM-5.3 went open-weight — 796 points, 277 comments. DeepSeek V4-Pro hit production Aug 12. "Semantic routing" — auto-dispatching each query to whichever model is currently best value — is now a normal thing developers do, which quietly ends model loyalty. **→ N5, F2.**

**9 · Unattended agents.** Meta's Muse Code (Aug 5) ships as a terminal agent designed to "plan, execute, debug and complete software projects with minimal human oversight." HN's *"The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations"* — 167 points, 97 comments. **→ F4.**

## 4. The rules — last week's eight, plus two

**R1 · End on the open element.** The last word carries the latch: *yet, still, Pick, Which, None of them.*

**R2 · No punchline.** A closing aphorism costs replies. If it's good, it's a reply *you* post underneath.

**R3 · Collectible over correct.** "Name one" beats "which one" beats "why".

**R4 · Every answer must be disputable by a stranger.** That's the multiplier.

**R5 · Seed the format, not the answer.** "Mine: …" demonstrates shape and length, never the right answer.

**R6 · The seed reply opens a new axis, never a conclusion.** Held from last week, and every seed below obeys it.

**R7 · Ban the essay ask.** No "why", no "what's your take", unless the honest answer fits in one clause.

**R8 · Ration the confession.** Five verdicts out of 28, all in a day's best slot.

**R9 · NEW — a dilemma must cost something on both sides.** If one option is obviously right it's a poll, not a fight. Test before you post: can you write a convincing seed reply arguing for the *other* option? If not, the dilemma is fake.

**R10 · NEW — the number must be inside the reader's reality.** §1.3. $40k, not $2M. The reader has to be able to picture being offered it.

## 7. Novelty and copy risk

**Retired** (fired within 14 days, checked against `posts_published`): every stream-D subject from last week (agents in your codebase, tools you stopped opening, AI code tells, things nobody used, what AI made harder, indie-hacker slogans, products you'd miss, things that stopped being moats); all four bake-offs (earned its money, one subscription, dead by 2028, first paying customer); all four word budgets (three words, one word wrapper, talk me out of it, scare me in one word); all five verdicts (51 vs half my age, three unread PRs, revenue ghost mode, whatever the agent picked in March, landing-page disclosure); all five news pegs (lockfiles, agent-watchers, local 27B, data-centre politics, LinkedIn slop). Plus the whole Aug 15–23 personal block — hospital, whiteboard, plumber, 386/1994, Romanian, son/med school, shoebox, grandmother, doctor-30-minutes-late, teaching a child in 2030, medical file, pension/401k/podcast, the 15:00–19:00 window, the badge, the accounting office, the economist.

**Two specific collisions I caught and worked around:**

- **The dilemma is not new to your account.** *"You can keep the salary you have now with no security at all, or half of it guaranteed for life. Pick."* fired Aug 23, and *"You get to keep exactly one — the 30 years / the body you had at 25 / the certainty"* fired Aug 17. Both are life-generic. **Every dilemma this week is in-niche and about the work**, which is the correction §2 made last week applied to a shape you'd only used the personal version of. I dropped a planned closing dilemma about trading experience for youth for exactly this reason — it was the Aug 17 post with new paint.
- **A2's disclosure post fires tonight.** So I moved the AI-authorship faction split off the board and replaced it with F4 (unattended agents), which is adjacent to nothing in the last fortnight.

**Copy risk, stated plainly.** X4 (sell for $40k vs a 5% shot at a million) shares a skeleton with i_mika_el's $2M/$50M post. The skeleton is the oldest one on the internet — it's "would you rather" — and the numbers, framing and seed are all yours, but it's the closest thing to a lift in the set, so it sits at Thu 23:46 rather than in an 02:xx marquee slot. Nothing reuses his *"half of devs / other half"* phrasing verbatim; the four F posts state their factions in your own words. No subject of @shirshakchavan's is reused at all — no browsers, no Notion/Obsidian, no laptop-vs-desktop, no milestone posts.

## 9. How to run it

**The seed reply is not optional.** Reply to your own post within 60 seconds. It seeds the thread so the first reply isn't a stranger's, it makes the post a 2-post thread with a second surface, and it proves you're present. Every seed above opens a new axis instead of answering the question — if you rewrite one, keep that property.

**New this week — the dilemma seeds are the load-bearing ones.** Look at X2, X4, X5 and X7: each seed challenges the *credibility* of one group of repliers rather than their opinion ("everyone answering 'the junior' — did you actually do it this year"). That is what converts a poll into an argument, and it's the difference between 40 comments and 200. Post those four seeds exactly as written before improvising.

**Answer every reply on the X, A and N posts.** The multiplier only fires when the comment section becomes a venue. Your reply to reply #4 causes replies #5–40.

**The N-stream has a shelf life, and it is shorter than usual.** N1 (Cursor) and N6 (the payout change) are pegged to a story that is still moving — if OpenAI and SpaceX settle, or X delays Sept 7, those two are the first to pull. The X, D, A and F posts keep indefinitely.

**Reruns are legitimate.** Daniel reran his 128K post verbatim after 19 days and got 15,941 views with a better ratio. If one of these lands, requeue it unchanged for late September. The rewrite is what kills reruns.

**Spike protocol** — >5k views in the first hour, or >2k in 30 minutes:
1. Cancel the rest of the day's generated slots.
2. Reply substantively to every commenter for 48h. This alone can double the event.
3. Morning-after quote tweet with the best reply you got — not with your own commentary.
4. Sequel question on day 3, same skeleton, adjacent subject.
5. Pin the winner for 72h.

**Never two of the same skeleton in one day.** The grid enforces it — every day runs four different streams.

**Expected yield.** 28 posts is one or two mid-hits and a lottery ticket. Judge the batch, not the row. Don't kill the dilemma if X1 lands flat on Monday — n=17 on someone else's account is evidence; n=1 on yours is noise.

## 10. What to measure next Monday

**First: harvest your own profile in `posts` mode** (§0). It is the difference between this document being analysis and being astrology. Two weeks of data are sitting there uncollected.

Once you have it, three questions, in order of what they'd change:

1. **Dilemma vs challenge board, on reply:like.** The whole set is a bet that stream X (7 posts) beats stream D (6 posts) on comments per like. On other people's accounts, D runs 1.84 and X runs 1.15 — but D's number comes from an account with 30× your reach, and X's mechanism doesn't depend on reach. **If X comes back above D on your account, the dilemma is the backbone from mid-September and the challenge board becomes the short-form filler.** If D wins, revert and treat this week as an expensive experiment.

2. **Views per character, again, with a cleaner test.** All six challenge boards are under 110 characters (64–102) and all five verdicts are over 215. That's a genuinely separated distribution, unlike last week's. If the sub-110 posts beat the 215+ posts on views, short wins and stream A gets cut to two next week. If the confessions win again, your account is carried by the confession and the length finding is a myth borrowed from bigger accounts.

3. **Did the news pegs pay?** Six posts anchored to events three days old or less — the highest news density of any set so far. Compare N-stream median views against X, D, A and F. **If the news pegs underperform, stop paying the research cost**: the pegs take the most work to write and are the only posts that expire.

And one thing to watch that isn't a metric: **Sept 7 changes what "worked" means.** From Monday, a post that gets 50,000 views from non-verified accounts is worth less than one that gets 3,000 from Premium subscribers on the home timeline. Every number you pull after that date is measuring a different game than the numbers before it. Keep the two eras separate when you compare weeks, or you'll draw a conclusion from a rule change and think it was a content finding.
